cited_evidence.text: AbstractOwing to superior strength-ductility combination and great potential for applications in extreme conditions, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure have drawn enormous attention. However, the FCC structure limits yield strength and makes the alloys unable to meet ever-increasing demands for exploring the universe. Here, we report a strategy to obtain FCC materials with outstanding mechanical properties in both ambient and cryogenic environments, via exploiting dynamic development of the interstitial-driven local chemical order (LCO). Dense laths composed of the multiscaled LCO domains evolve from planar-slip bands that form in the prior thermomechanical processing, contributing to ultrahigh yield strengths over a wide temperature range. During cryogenic tensile deformation, LCO further develops and promotes remarkable dislocation cross-slip. Together with the deformation-driven transformation and twinning, these factors lead to satisfactory work hardening. AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility, including the easy motion of Shockley partials, their interactions to form stacking-fault parallelepipeds, and arrest at planar slip bands of undissociated dislocations. We further show that crack propagation is impeded by twinned, nanoscale bridges that form between the near-tip crack faces and delay fracture by shielding the crack tip. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has progressed from empirical alloy design to a more fundamental understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Recent studies have focused on the role of dislocations, short-range ordering, and local chemical order in controlling the strength and ductility of these alloys. The use of advanced characterization techniques, such as in-situ neutron diffraction and electron nanodiffraction, has enabled the study of these phenomena at the atomic scale.
decision.unsolved: Despite significant progress, the relationship between the atomic-scale structure and the macroscopic mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys is not yet fully understood. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms controlling the strength and ductility of these alloys, particularly in extreme environments such as high temperatures and cryogenic conditions.
decision.lever: ab initio calculations and in-situ transmission electron microscopy
decision.why: To further understand the relationship between local chemical order and mechanical properties, ab initio calculations can be used to model the dynamic development of local chemical order, while in-situ transmission electron microscopy can provide real-time observations of dislocation behavior and deformation mechanisms. This combined approach can help to reveal the underlying mechanisms controlling the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys.
